tagline: Follow a freight canal through industrial cities and surviving canal towns
intro: The Ohio & Erie Canalway drive links Cleveland’s neighborhoods and industrial districts with the Cuyahoga Valley and canal towns farther south. The Federal Highway Administration lists this 110-mile route as a National Scenic Byway, allowing four and a half hours for the drive. Its description emphasizes working rivers, industrial landscapes and natural areas, with journeys by trail and train as well as road.

The canal supplied the earlier transportation corridor. Engineer James Geddes, who had worked on New York’s canals, was hired to design the system. Construction began in 1825, and the first boat traveled from Akron to Cleveland in July 1827. Completion in 1832 connected Cleveland with the Ohio River at Portsmouth. Railroads drew business away, while the canal continued supplying water to factories and towns. The 1913 flood destroyed aqueducts, banks and locks; a few sections nevertheless continued carrying local cargo afterward.

From Cleveland, three branches pass through historic neighborhoods, the industrial area or the Warehouse District before reaching Cuyahoga Valley National Park. Continue south through Akron’s Cascade Locks and Barberton to Canal Fulton. Massillon has the spur to Canton; the main journey continues through Navarre and Zoar to New Philadelphia. A bicycle and pedestrian trail follows the old towpath route in the Cleveland and Akron area.

moments.title: Cascade Locks, Akron
moments.text: Twenty-one locks made two miles of canal through Akron a six-hour boat journey. Cascade Locks occupied the steepest grade on the canal, in a ravine northwest of downtown. The stops at each lock brought time for trade, while the parallel Crosby’s Mill Race supplied hydraulic power to industry. The 1913 flood badly damaged the locks. A footpath now runs beside them, and the Mustill Store serves as a visitor center and canal museum. The district also contains two railroad bridges across the gorge and the site of Ferdinand Schumacher’s original mills.
moments.notice: A footpath follows the locks; the Mustill Store is a visitor center and canal museum.

moments.title: Canal Fulton
moments.text: St. Helena III puts a reproduction canal boat back on the water at Canal Fulton. Ohio’s byway story map describes a mule-drawn, two-and-a-half-mile round-trip tour, with canal-era memorabilia at the Heritage House/Old Canal Days Museum. The town itself grew from settlements on the Tuscarawas River. Canal construction between 1826 and 1828 brought Fulton into being across the river from Milan. Fulton added “Canal” to its name in 1832 and absorbed Milan and West Fulton in 1853. The Canalway Visitor Center supplies interpretation of the town and canal, with the boat tours as a central feature.

moments.title: Zoar
moments.text: Digging the canal helped Zoar’s communal society pay for its land. German religious dissenters founded the Society of Separatists of Zoar in 1817. They had bought land sight unseen with loans to repay; when Ohio needed a canal right of way, it offered them paid excavation work. That work allowed them to clear the debt on time. Elected trustees had managed the society’s farms, shops and factories, with all property held in common. The society dissolved in 1898, dividing its property among the remaining residents. Much of the early village layout and many buildings survive.
moments.notice: Much of Zoar’s early layout and many buildings from its communal period survive.
